verdicts.quote: The spreadsheet step is automatically triggered when the nurse saves the ward note in the system — no extra action needed. ... the same note must appear in ShareSheet by 8 a.m. the next day.

The ward manager gets an email alert every morning at 7:30 a.m. with a list of patients who have new notes since the previous day, including a link to view the note and download the updated spreadsheet.
If a nurse forgets to enter a note, the system sends a reminder to them and their team leader at 10 a.m. the next day.
The spreadsheet step is automatically triggered when the nurse saves the ward note in the system — no extra action needed.

If a note isn’t entered by 10 a.m. the next day, it stays in the system as a pending task for the nurse, but the team leader gets an alert at 10:15 a.m. with the nurse’s name and patient full name. ... The alert includes a direct link to the note entry page. ... If the note still isn’t entered by 11 a.m., the system logs it as a delay in the quality team’s weekly report — but only if it's the second time in a week for that nurse.
The finance supervisor also uses it once a month to match nurse hours with documented patient interactions.
If there’s any delay in syncing the note to ShareSheet, the system should log it with a timestamp and alert the IT team within 5 minutes, so we don’t lose track of it.

The note stays in the system on their device, and the system automatically retries every 5 minutes for up to 30 minutes. If it still fails after that, the system shows a second message: “Still unable to send. Please contact IT now.” At the same time, the IT team gets an alert with the nurse’s name, patient ID, and time of failure.

Yes — when the first note is saved and ShareSheet is unreachable, the nurse should see a clear message on screen: “Note saved locally, but not yet sent to ShareSheet. Please check again in 5 minutes.” ... If it still fails after 30 minutes, the system shows a second message: “Still unable to send. Please contact IT now.”

The system must also prevent nurses from editing a note after 48 hours — once it’s been synced, it’s final, unless a supervisor approves a correction. ... If a nurse needs to correct a note, they must add a new one with a timestamp and explanation, not overwrite the original.
The system should flag any edit after 48 hours and send it to the team leader for review.

No, the team leader had no way to see it was missing before 8:15 a.m. — there was no dashboard or alert system at that time. ... That’s why the 10:15 a.m. alert is so important — it’s not just for the nurse, it’s for the team leader to catch problems early.

When the ward manager opens the system each morning, the first thing they see is a summary dashboard with three key items: the number of notes entered so far today, how many are overdue (more than 10 a.m.), and a list of nurses who haven’t entered a note yet.
The manager then sends a quick message through the system to the nurse — no phone calls needed — saying “Hi, just checking in on your notes for Mr. Smith. Thanks!”
If a nurse has missed two notes in a row, the manager gets a yellow alert and can schedule a quick 5-minute huddle to check in.
If they’re new to the system, they get a short video pop-up the first time, but only once.
The team leader gets an alert at 10:15 a.m. with the nurse’s name, the missing patient, and the time. The alert includes a direct link to the note entry page.
If a note still isn’t entered by 9:30 a.m., the system escalates it to the ward manager automatically.

The first thing the care coordinator looks for is the list of patients who have new notes from the previous day — specifically, any patient with a note marked “urgent” or “new assessment” — because that’s what drives their task planning.
